about: The words of the chain pilgrim_road (Data/encounters/chain_pilgrim_road_793.json; Design/content/chains/pilgrim_road.md): the English road to Rome by way of Quentovic, a Kentish widow, the priest in her party who is of the old Kentish kings' kin (Eadberht, later called Praen), the toll house and the cell of Saint Josse, and what a pilgrim brings back. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', with '_success' and '_failure' where there is a chance, named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the two news items the endings post; one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture and one 'art.chain_pilgrim_road.ending.<name>' for each ending. People: Osmund the guest-master and Hildric the clerk (places/quentovic.json), Hereberht the reeve (places/dofras.json), Cwenburh the nun and the toll man (places/sarre.json), Sigewine, Beornwine, Ravn and the reeve Wighelm (the spine's cast); Wilburh the widow and Heahstan the steward are ordinary invented people; Eadberht Praen, King Offa, King Coenwulf, King Charles, Alcuin and his priest Martin are historical. Nothing is quoted: the Chronicle's sentences in the intentions ('This year ...') are our own plain renderings of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's entries for 796 and 798, in its manner. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Three for the Apostles
A widow, her mass-priest and a girl wait above the tide line with staffs and bundles. They want a keel to Cwantawic, and the priest keeps his back to the road.
We are three for the thresholds of the Apostles: myself, my mass-priest and the girl. We want a keel to Cwantawic. After that we have feet.
My husband is three winters dead and the sea has my son. I have prayed for them in every church in Kent. There is one church left that I have not tried.
We came up to the Strand to find a ship. In Kent every keel is counted out and counted in, and I did not care to be counted.
Two skippers have said no since Sunday. One looked at the reeve's house before he said it.
God keep your boat, shipman. I can pull an oar, if that changes the reckoning.
Take them for a fare: ten pennies a head
Take them for nothing but a prayer at the tomb
You are not bound that way: hear their road and wish them a keel
The widow counts thirty pennies into your hand without haggling. The girl is sick before the boat is off the shingle. The priest sits in the bow and watches the shore until there is none.
The widow says your name over twice so as to have it right when she gets there. The crew find room. The priest sits in the bow and watches the shore until there is none.

They mean to walk from the Canche to Rome before the snow shuts the mountain. The widow says the ports of Kent are watched for people who leave without the king's leave, and looks at her priest when she says it. You hear later that a Frank took them over on the next tide.
A priest who pulls an oar
Mid-channel the wind drops. The widow's priest takes an oar unasked and pulls it like a man raised to it. When the bread goes round, the widow serves him before herself.
He is a priest right enough. He says the hours under his breath and gets them right, which is more than our own priest did at Gyrwe.
But a lady does not hand her mass-priest the bread first. She did it without thinking. People only do that for one kind of man.
My father thought a boy should know a boat, a horse and a psalter. I kept two of the three.
He is my priest. That is what he is on this boat.
Ask him straight who he is
Say nothing and watch what the widow does
Leave him be and ask the widow about her road

A priest, he says. Then, since there is water all round: a priest whose father's father sat in the king's seat at Canterbury, before Kent had a Mercian for its king. King Offa would like him nearer to hand. He asks you to have forgotten it by the Canche.
When the coast of Kent goes under the sea's edge the widow bows her head to him, not to the shore, and he lets her. Your lookout sees it too. Whatever the man is, Kent used to bow to it.
The widow sleeps. The priest pulls his oar. The girl is sick again. You learn nothing, which is what they paid for.

Eleven weeks' walking, she has been told, if nothing goes wrong: Saint-Riquier, Saint-Denis, the long plain, then the mountain of Jove, which is crossed before the snow or not until after it. Then Pavia, where everything is for sale, and Rome. By Saint Peter's there is a street of English with a church of their own. You can die there among people who understand what you say.
A priest without a letter
At the toll house on the Canche the clerk waves the widow and the girl through without looking up: pilgrims pay nothing. Then he looks up, and asks the priest for his bishop's letter.
Pilgrims for Rome pay no toll, at this house or any bridge or ferry in the kingdom. That is old King Pippin's law. I did not make it.
But a priest away from his own church carries his bishop's letter, or nobody is to take him in. That is the present king's law. I did not make that either.
And since the two kings wrote to each other I am to open pilgrims' bundles as well, for cloaks. Your people have made my mornings longer.
You brought them over, Frisian. Do you speak for him?
The man who brought them put them on the bank and went out on the same tide. So nobody speaks for him. Unless you do; I saw her greet you.
I had a letter. It went into the water at the beach, with one of my shoes.
My bishop is King Offa's man. He would have written me a letter, and it would have been to the king's hall at Tamworth.
He is my mass-priest and says the office for my dead. I answer for him. Write my name down, if you want a name.
Swear that he is the widow's priest and no trader
Lay fifteen pennies on his table for the trouble of not writing
It is not your business: let him write the name down

The clerk takes your oath the way he would take it for your own goods, and puts his stylus down. He says a skipper who swears for strangers ought at least to have his cargo looked at kindly, and tells the toll man so.
The clerk hears the oath out and writes all the same: a priest of Kent, no letter, sworn for by a Frisian. He reads it back to you. He says it is nothing. The abbot only likes his tablets full.
The clerk looks at the fifteen pennies and then at the ceiling. He smooths the wax with his thumb. He says three pilgrims passed, he thinks, or it may have been two.

The clerk writes: a priest of Kent, no letter. He asks the name and the priest gives it: Eadberht. The tablets go to the abbot at the month's end, and the abbot is the English king's friend. The priest watches the stylus as if it were being used on him.
The saint's guests

A league down the bank the cell of Saint Josse takes in whoever comes over the sea. Pilgrims sit along the south wall with their staffs. The widow counts her silver twice, and it is the same both times.
King Charles gave this house to my master Alcuin so that pilgrims should be fed. He did not give a mule with it. I mention it because everybody asks.

A company leaves on Monday for Saint-Riquier and Saint-Denis. With a mule she keeps up with it and is over the mountain before the snow. On foot she winters on this side, and people who winter on this side mostly go home.
Martin, the abbot's own priest, lies sick in our guest hall this autumn. We are short of everything but patience, and I am watching the patience.
They say our saint's hair still grows in his coffin, and that his keepers cut it. I keep the guests. Nobody has handed me the shears.
I have enough to reach Rome, or enough to come back from it. I had not reckoned what a mule costs among the Franks.
Lend her sixty pennies for a mule, to be settled when she comes back
Give the cell twelve pennies for the pilgrims' pot
Wish her a dry road: the monks will see to her

The widow takes the sixty pennies and cuts a tally for them herself, badly. She says she will pay you in whatever Rome sells that Kent does not. The guest-master says he has seen that promise kept about one time in two, and that the other time is not the pilgrim's fault.

The guest-master puts the twelve pennies in the pot box and says the house pays its debts in what it has. What it has is a riddle of Bishop Aldhelm's about a tower that shows ships their road. He says there is such a tower a day north of here, and it has been dark longer than anyone has been alive.

The widow thanks you for the crossing and goes in to supper. The guest-master walks you to the fence. If you come this way again, he says, bring wax: the saint's lights eat it and the house will pay over the common price until Martinmas.
Half a penny
At dusk the priest walks you back along the bank. He is going no further than the Frankish king's hall, he says: Rome will wait for him. He holds out half of a cut penny.
This is a penny of King Ecgberht, the last king Kent had of its own. You will not have seen many. A man at Dofras has the other half.
His name is Heahstan and he buys wine for a thegn's hall. Put it in his hand and say: the priest is over the water. Nothing else. He will know how much that is.
You know what I am. So you know why it cannot go by a Kentish boat.
I am a priest. I was born something else as well, and King Offa remembers which. That is as much as is good for you.
My name is on that clerk's wax now, and wax travels. So it must go soon.
Take the half penny
Take it, and ask what a king's kinsman pays a ferryman
Give it back: you carry goods, not kingdoms
The half penny weighs nothing. He closes your hand over it with both of his, the way a priest does with something else, and walks back toward the cell without looking round.

He gives you twenty pennies, which by the look of his purse is most of them. When Kent has a king again, he says, your keel will pay nothing between the two Forelands. He has nothing else to promise with, and says so.
He closes his hand on it. Then you carried a widow's priest over the sea, he says, and that is all you did. He does not seem angry. He seems to be counting who is left to ask.
Two men on the shingle
At Dofras a steward is buying wine on the shingle and taking his time over it. Twenty paces off the king's reeve is asking each skipper whom he carried over this summer.
The king wishes to know who leaves Kent without his leave. Priests above all. I only ask the question. I am a Kentish man myself, as people keep reminding me.
There is silver for a true answer. The king's silver, not mine. I would not spend mine on it.
A tablet came over from the Franks' toll house with a Kentish priest on it and a Frisian keel beside him. No letter, it says. I thought you might help me read it.
I buy for a hall that used to drink with kings and now drinks with whoever calls. Show me what you have, Frisian. Slowly; I am old.
Bargain with the steward over wine you have not got, and pass the half penny with the handshake
Tell the reeve whom you carried, and show him the half penny
Do neither: the half penny goes over the side at the first deep water

You say the words into the handshake. Heahstan's face does nothing at all. He pays forty pennies in front of everyone for two casks of Frankish wine that you are to bring him before the winter, and complains of the price loudly enough for the reeve to hear.

The half penny goes across. So does the reeve, a moment later: he has seen a handshake that lasted too long. He finds nothing on either of you, because Heahstan has swallowed it. He takes twenty pennies from you for selling unwitnessed, and he will know your boat again.

The reeve turns the half penny over for some time. He says he had hoped nobody would answer. Then he counts out a hundred and twenty pennies, the king's, exactly. When you look round the steward has gone, and has left his wine standing on the shingle.
You tell the reeve you carry wine and stones. You tell the steward the price of wine. Off the South Foreland the half penny goes into forty feet of water, where the last king of Kent can keep it.
Word from the thresholds

A Northumbrian monk with sore feet and a satchel of letters finds your boat. He has walked from Rome by Tours, and one of his messages is by word of mouth, for the Frisian who carried a widow of Kent.

She reached Rome. The girl did not come away from it: the fever in that city takes the young ones first. She lies in the English quarter by Saint Peter's, where our people have their own church and their own graves, and need both.
The widow has it too, the kind that comes back every third day. On the days between she is well and does everything she went there to do. She has done most of it twice.
She will start north when the mountain opens. Look for her at Saint Josse about four months from now. If your boat is not there she will wait. She says she has learned how.
I was to tell you, in these words, that it was a good mule.

There are Frisians there as well, with a house of their own under the hill. At the tomb of the Apostle one of them asked me what herring was fetching at Dorestad. I did not know. He was disappointed in me.
The old pope died at Christmas. The new one is called Leo, and the Romans have not yet made up their minds about him. When Romans make up their minds it is as well to be elsewhere.
Send forty pennies south by the next company, for her road home
Send word only: the boat will be at the Canche
Promise the boat, and ask him what became of the priest

The monk sews the forty pennies into a hem for the next company going south and writes her name on a scrap to go with them. He says about half of what is sent that way arrives. He says it as a man who has thought about which half.
The monk repeats the message until he has it: the boat will be at the Canche. He says it is the shortest letter he has carried this year and the only one he has understood.

The priest left the company at Saint-Denis and went to the king. King Charles feeds a number of Englishmen who cannot go home, the monk says; King Offa has asked for them more than once, and is answered politely. For the asking he gives you a riddle he has no room to carry: Bishop Aldhelm's, about a chest full of books that has never read one.
What she brought back
The widow sits against the south wall of the cell with her staff across her knees. She is half the weight she was. The girl's bundle lies beside her own.
This cloth lay a night on the Apostle's tomb. They weigh it before and after, and it comes up heavier. I watched the scale myself. I do not understand it and found I did not need to.
At Pavia I sold the gold-worked bands I took for the road, and bought what a Kentish church cannot get: pepper, incense, a little silk for an altar. Everyone does. The Lombards have a street for us.
And I have a fever, the girl's shoes, and the right way to sing the Alleluia, which is not how we sing it at home. I have been asked what a pilgrim brings back. That is the list.
I owe you a mule. It died under the mountain, on the way back, so it did all that was asked of it.
Your forty pennies found me at Saint-Maurice, under the pass. I ate them. I thought you would rather know that than be thanked.

A sealed leaf was left here at Candlemas by a priest from the king's hall, for the first of Kent to come back this way. She is the first. I gave it to her this morning, and she has been holding it like a hot dish since.
Take her home, and take the pepper and incense she offers against the mule
Take her home for a length of the silk
Take her home for nothing

She measures out two bags of pepper and two of incense on the guest-master's scale and will not be told it is too much. A debt carried over the mountain grows, she says. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
She cuts you a length of the altar silk without a word and folds what is left smaller. It is good silk. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
She says nothing for a while. Then she says she has met four kinds of people on the road and had begun to think there were only three. She comes down to the boat on the monk's arm.
The third day
Off the Frankish shore the widow's fever comes back on its day. She lies under the bottom boards with her teeth shut and shakes the boat. The crew look at her, and then at you.
It is the third-day fever. The brothers at Gyrwe had it from the marsh. It does not pass from one man to the next. I think it does not.
You think it does not. Well. She walked to the end of the world and back for a rag. I would not put her ashore, not her. I would not sit next to her either.
It will be gone by dark. It always is. Sail your boat.
Put your own cloak over her and hold the course
Let the lookout ask her to lay the cloth against the mast
Heave to, rig the sail over her and lose the tide

You steer in your shirt until dark. The crew say nothing about it, in the way that means they are saying a good deal. By dark the shaking stops, as she said it would, and she hands the cloak back folded.

She has the cloth held to the mast for the space of a psalm. The wind comes round fair before the psalm is done. Ravn says winds do that. He says it quietly, and afterwards he is seen to touch the mast in passing.
She has the cloth held to the mast for the space of a psalm. Nothing changes but the light. Ravn says nothing in a way that everyone hears. The fever goes at dark, as it always does.
The sail comes down and goes over her like a roof. The boat lies beam on and rolls for half a day. Nobody complains: a crew will forgive a lost tide sooner than a sick woman left in the wet.
The sealed leaf

At Sarre the widow kneels on the strand until the nun from the ship-house lifts her up. Then she takes the priest's sealed leaf out of her bundle and asks you what to do with it, because she can no longer tell what is a pilgrim's business.
He asks me to see it to Heahstan's lord. I have carried heavier things further, and none I liked less.
I went to pray for two dead. I think this leaf is for making more. But I served him the bread first, on your boat; you saw me. So I am not the one to judge it.
They tell me at the toll that Kent has a king, and that he was a priest. Then the leaf is late, and I still know whose hand it must go to.
They tell me at the toll how it ended, and what was done to his hands. Then this is a letter to nobody. I would still like it somewhere that is not my bundle.
If it is given into the abbess's hand it goes into the house's chest with the old kings' charters, unopened. What goes into that chest stays there. We have kept worse things than a letter.

I hear a widow has come home from Rome. The king is glad of every pilgrim's safe return, and of anything a pilgrim may have been given to carry. I have a horse, and I can wait as long as the ferry can.
See the leaf over the ferry to the hall it is meant for
Take the leaf over the ferry yourself, under the eyes of the king's man
Give the leaf to the king's man
Tell her it is no pilgrim's business, and let the abbess's chest have it

The ferryman takes it over inside his shirt with a load of oysters and comes back without it. He asks no question and is given a penny for that. The widow watches the far bank until the road is empty.

You cross with a cask on your shoulder and the leaf under your belt. The king's man watches the cask the whole way over. On the Canterbury side a boy takes the leaf from you and is gone into the saltings before you have set the cask down.

The king's man rides down into the ford and has the ferry held. Before he reaches it the leaf is over the side, and the Wantsum takes ink as readily as anything else. He fines you thirty pennies for crossing without the toll man's word, and looks at the water for some time.

The king's man breaks the seal there on the strand and reads standing. He counts two hundred pennies into your hand without looking at them. The widow does not speak to you. The nun takes her up the bank, and neither of them turns round.

The widow lets out her breath. The nun takes the leaf between two fingers and carries it up to the ship-house as if it might spill. On her way she has a word with the toll man about your keel, and he finds he can count it at the half for a while.
The priest is over the water

This year King Offa died, three days before Lammas, and before the corn was in Kent had a king of its own again. The men at the toll post say he was a priest. A steward is waiting on the strand with a horse for you.
He came ashore with nine men. By the second Sunday he had the hall at Canterbury and the archbishop had taken ship. The archbishop was King Offa's man and nobody had to tell him so.
The leaf told six halls to be ready and for what day. They were ready. I am not a young man and I rode all night, and I would do it again.
I told you once that you had carried a widow's priest and that was all. I was wrong, and I have seldom been so glad of it.
I have had pennies struck with my name on them. A king must, or he is only a man in a hall. Take some. The silver is good, whatever comes to be said of the name.
I promised your keel something on the bank of the Canche, when I had nothing. I have it to give now. Hold me to it quickly.
They will say a priest threw off his gown to put on a ring. It is true. Kent had nobody else left to ask.
Ask for his writing: your keel free of toll in the Wantsum
Take the writing and a place among his men, as the one who carried the half penny and helped the widow
Take his new pennies and Heahstan's friendship, and nothing with your name on it

A clerk writes it while you wait: this man's keel passes Sarre and Fordwic without toll, as the old kings granted to the minster's ships. The king makes his cross under it. Six hundred of the new pennies go into your chest. Your name is on a king's writing, in a year when Kent has changed kings once already.

The king has the writing made, and then has you sit at his table, three places down. Heahstan says the men above you have land and the men below you have swords, and that you are the only one who came by boat. Twelve hundred pennies, and a name the Kentish will know as long as this king sits there.

The king laughs for the first time and says a Frisian is a hard man to reward. Nine hundred pennies, new from the die. Heahstan walks you down to the boat: whatever you leave in his storehouse at Dofras will be there when you come back, and so, he hopes, will he.
Kent kept quiet
This year King Offa died, three days before Lammas. In Kent, where men had waited ten years for that day, nobody stirred. The reeve has a bag for you that has been sealed for some time.
There were six names in that leaf. The king had the men brought to him before he died, and their sons with them. He killed none of them. He was old and wanted it quiet.
So when he died there was nobody in Kent to light the fire, and a priest at the Frankish king's table with no one to come home to. He is there yet. I am told he says Mass well.
The new king has not needed to bring an army into Kent. He has you to thank for that and does not know your name. I have kept it so. You may thank me or not.
The widow went into the minster on Thanet. She does not ask after you. In Kent they do, now and then, and I would beach elsewhere than the Wantsum for a year or two.
Take the bag, and the king's protection for your house
Take the bag, and ask for ground on the Strand at Lundenwic
Take the protection, and send half the bag to Saint Josse for the men who cannot come home

Eight hundred pennies, and the reeve's word before witnesses that your house and its goods stand under the king's hand in every Mercian port. No fire was lit in Kent that year or the next. Nobody will ever be able to say what that was worth, which the reeve says is the best kind of service and the worst paid.

Six hundred pennies, and the reeve paces out a plot above the Strand himself, twelve of his rods by four. He drives the corner stakes with his own heel. He says it is good ground, and that he would not tell the neighbours how you came by it.

You keep four hundred and the king's protection. The other four hundred go over the water to the guest-master at Saint Josse, for the Englishmen who eat at the Frankish king's table and cannot go home. He sends back no thanks, only a tally with the sum cut in it, exactly.
Written in the book
The widow has given her land to the minster and taken the veil there. The nun who keeps the ships comes down to your boat with a tablet, a purse and a folded strip of cloth.
She has sold her husband's horse and his war-gear and says the price is yours. I told her it was too much. She told me I had not been there.
The leaf is in the chest. Nobody has opened it, and nobody will in my time. I have written on the lid what it is, in case the next keeper is curious, and what I think of curiosity.
You sent the leaf over the ferry, I know. It came to whatever it came to without you. That happens to most letters.
Kent has a king of its own this year. It did not need that leaf to get him. It will need a great deal more than a leaf to keep him.
They took the priest who was king, down in the Marsh, and led him into Mercia bound. I pray for him. I also count the house's ships each evening, and all of them are there.
I have the fever still, every third day, and have stopped minding it. The sisters have learned the Alleluia my way. Come and be prayed for when you pass; it costs nothing here.
Take the purse, and ask that your keel sail under the abbess's cross
Take the purse, and the strip of the cloth for under the mast
She says the one who asked no fare is to have both, and the minster's wine to fetch
Ask only that your dead be written in the minster's book

Six hundred and fifty pennies. The nun nails a small wooden cross to your stem herself and enters your keel on her tablet among the house's ships. The old king's charter allows the minster a ship in place of one worn out, she says, and the toll man has never yet won an argument with it.

Six hundred and fifty pennies, and a strip of the cloth two fingers wide, sewn into a linen bag. It goes under the mast, where a coin goes when a keel is new. The crew watch it go in. Even Ravn finds something to do nearby.

Twelve hundred pennies, the cross on your stem, the strip of cloth under your mast, and the minster's order for six casks of Frankish wine at better than the common price. The nun reads the list out twice, as if hoping to find a mistake in it. The widow, she says, was very exact.

The nun writes your father's name and your mother's on her tablet and asks how they are said. They will be read out at Minster with the house's own dead, each year, for as long as there are sisters to read. She leaves the purse on your thwart all the same: six hundred and fifty pennies. The widow said you would try to refuse it.
After the Marsh
This year King Coenwulf laid Kent waste as far as the Marsh, took the priest who was its king, and led him bound into Mercia. At the toll post a Mercian sits beside the toll man with a list.
They put out his eyes and cut off his hands. A priest's hands. He can be neither king nor priest now, and that was the thought behind it.
King Coenwulf's brother has Kent. Every writing the priest gave is void. Some men's names are on those writings, and I have them here.

Yours is one. A keel free of toll in the Wantsum. The new king may be brought to say the same thing in his own name, for a hundred and fifty pennies. He is a reasonable lord, and new, and short of silver.
Yours is not. You had his pennies, I am told. So did half of Kent. We are melting them.
They say he is alive, in a minster in the west, and that somebody feeds him. I do not ask who says so.
Buy the new king's word over the old writing: a hundred and fifty pennies
Let the writing lapse and keep your silver
Say that you sold the man wine, like half of Kent
Ask where the priest is kept, and send thirty pennies for his keep

The Mercian scrapes one king's name off the leaf and writes another over it. The cross beneath is new and the words are the same. Your keel still passes free. The toll man says a writing is like a boat: it is the same boat, whoever is steering.

The Mercian draws a line through your name and looks almost sorry: it was a good writing. From today your keel pays at Sarre and Fordwic like any other. The toll man holds out his hand, to show there is no ill will in it.

The Mercian runs his finger down the list twice and does not find you. He says a man who takes pennies and no parchment has either no ambition or a great deal of sense. The toll man says that with Frisians it is hard to tell.

The toll man knows a carter who knows a monk. Your thirty pennies go west with a load of salt. Some weeks later word comes back the same way: the man they keep there could not see who had sent it, and asked to have the name said twice.

Offa, king of the Mercians, is dead, and the Kentish have taken a king of their own kin, Eadberht, whom they call Praen, the priest. The archbishop has left Canterbury. English ships are slow to sail until it is known whose toll is whose.
Offa, king of the Mercians, is dead. Men looked for a rising in Kent and none came: the Wantsum ports trade as before, and the Mercian reeves sit where they sat.

A shingle strand in Kent, a bright windy morning: a thin widow of about forty-five in an undyed cloak and linen head-cloth, a staff in her hand and a roped bundle at her feet; beside her a girl of fifteen; a little apart, a tonsured man in a plain dark gown with his back to the track; a small beached boat in front.

Mid-channel in a flat calm, noon, the sail hanging: a tonsured priest pulling an oar with a rower's back; the widow holding out bread to him first; in the bow a young English lookout watching the two of them instead of the sea.

The toll house on the Canche, grey morning light through open doors: a Frankish clerk at a long table with wax tablets, his stylus pointed at the priest; the widow and the girl already past him in the doorway; a balance hanging from the beam.

The cell of Saint Josse, late afternoon sun: pilgrims with staffs sitting in a row against the south wall of a small church; an English monk carrying a pot of pulses; the widow counting pennies in her lap; dunes and the river mouth behind.
The bank of the Canche at dusk, the tide out: the priest holding out half of a cut silver penny on his open palm to the skipper; beached boats and one lantern behind them; the first stars.

The shingle at Dofras under the grey Roman wall, overcast noon: in front an old steward tasting wine from a horn beside casks; twenty paces behind, a reeve with a rod of office questioning a skipper; the skipper of the small boat between them, one hand closed.

A jetty at a Frankish river port, a wet afternoon: a lean Northumbrian monk sitting on the boat's gunwale with his shoes off and a satchel of letters on his knees, talking; the skipper listening with a rope in his hands.

The south wall of the cell of Saint Josse, clear morning: the widow, grown gaunt and brown, sitting with her staff across her knees; two bundles beside her, one small with a pair of girl's shoes tied to it; in her hands a folded cloth and a sealed leaf of parchment; the guest-master standing by.

The open boat under sail off a low shore, late afternoon, a grey chop: the widow lying under a cloak on the bottom boards, shaking; three crewmen turned toward the skipper at the steering oar; a strip of pale cloth in her fist.

The strand at Sarre, evening light on the mud: the widow on her knees being raised by a nun in an undyed gown; in the widow's hand a sealed leaf held out to the skipper; on the bank above, a horseman sitting still beside the toll post.

A timber hall in Kent by firelight, a harvest evening: the priest of the boat, now in a red cloak with a gold ring on his hand and his tonsure growing out, pressing a handful of new pennies on the skipper; an old steward smiling behind; spears stacked by the door.
A reeve's house above a beach, a dull still afternoon: a sealed leather bag on a table between the reeve and the skipper; through the open door a quiet strand with boats unloading and nobody armed.

The abbess's ship-house at Sarre, a clear cold morning: a nun with a wax tablet handing down a purse and a folded strip of cloth into the boat; on the bank above, a veiled widow leaning on a staff, one hand raised.
The toll post at a Kentish landing in autumn rain: a Mercian in a good cloak sitting beside the grey toll man with a parchment list on his knee, his finger on a name; smoke on the skyline inland.
A silver penny with a king's name on it lying beside half of an older cut penny, on a boat's thwart; behind, a Kentish strand with a hall's smoke rising.
An empty beacon stack on a chalk headland at sunset, unlit, the firewood grown over with grass; below it a calm strait full of ordinary sails.
An open book of names on a lectern in a small wooden church, a nun's finger on a line; through the door a boat with a little cross on her stem lying at a strand.
